claims.note: CSIS warns that during a US-China war Russia, North Korea or Iran 'might take advantage of U.S. distraction', the same opportunism mechanism but in the reverse direction from the claim.

claims.text: Great wars often start through accident and miscalculation rather than deliberate plans
claims.note: Historians debate it: miscalculation mattered in 1914, but most major wars also involved deliberate decisions.

claims.text: The world is closer to nuclear war now than at any time since the Cuban Missile Crisis
claims.note: The Doomsday Clock is at its closest ever and arms control has lapsed, but few experts rate today's risk above the worst Cold War crises.

claims.text: The US president alone can order a nuclear launch
claims.note: US command and control gives the president sole authority to order nuclear use without the consent of Congress or the cabinet.

claims.text: Launch-on-warning policies make an accidental nuclear war more likely
claims.note: Launch on warning acts on a single sensor family and the paper calls it 'more error-prone' than launch under attack, which needs confirmation from both satellite and radar; the model assumes both sides shift to it in crises.

claims.text: US missile defences could not stop a large-scale nuclear attack
claims.note: US homeland defence has 44 ground-based interceptors designed against a few North Korean missiles, not a Russian salvo.

claims.text: A regional nuclear war between India and Pakistan could cause a global famine
claims.note: Climate models project large crop losses from such a war, but soot estimates and outcomes are contested.

claims.text: The US is raising its defence budget because it expects a major war
claims.note: SIPRI finds US military spending fell 7.5 percent in 2025 to $954 billion, mainly because supplemental aid to Ukraine stopped; its stated priorities are nuclear modernization and deterring China, not preparing for an expected major war.

claims.text: The US cannot survive a global conflict if Russia and China are aligned against it
claims.note: The US and its allies outweigh Russia and China in economic output and naval power; the claim is a sweeping assertion.

claims.text: Russia and China have formed a military alliance
claims.note: DoD 2025: despite deeper ties, Beijing and Moscow 'remain unwilling to establish a formal defense alliance with mutual security guarantees', still distrust each other, and China has withheld lethal aid for Russia's war.

claims.text: NATO is finished [2026]
claims.note: NATO still functions: all 32 members met at the 2026 summit and Article 5 stands, though US commitment has weakened.

claims.text: Rising gold and silver prices show investors expect a major war
claims.note: Precious metals rose on central-bank buying, interest rates and currency worries; prices do not single out war.

claims.text: Nostradamus predicted a third world war
claims.note: The quatrains are vague verse read after the fact; none names a third world war, its date or its parties, and no reading has forecast a war before it happened.

claims.text: Nostradamus accurately predicted Napoleon and Hitler
claims.note: 'Hister' is the Latin name of the Danube and the Napoleon anagram needs letter swaps; the matches were fitted after the events.

claims.text: The return of Jews to Israel fulfils biblical end-times prophecy
claims.note: Reading modern Israel as a sign of the end times is religious interpretation that no evidence can settle.

claims.text: The number of nuclear weapons held by rogue states is rising fast
claims.note: North Korea, the only such state with nuclear weapons, has grown its arsenal to an estimated few dozen warheads, but Iran has none and no other rogue state has built one.

claims.text: The 2026 US-Israeli war with Iran will be short, lasting weeks rather than years
claims.note: The 2026 war ran from 28 February to a ceasefire on 8 April, about forty days, though talks were unsettled and a resumption was possible.

claims.text: China will not start a crisis over Taiwan in 2026
claims.note: As of October 2026 China had not blockaded or attacked Taiwan and a Trump-Xi summit eased tensions, though the year is not over.

claims.text: US munitions and interceptor stocks are too shallow for a long high-intensity war
claims.note: In every CSIS iteration the US used up its entire global inventory of about 450 LRASM anti-ship missiles in the first week of the war.

claims.text: The US and Taiwan are not investing enough to deter a Chinese attack on Taiwan
claims.note: Taiwan's defence spending stayed near 2.5% of GDP and US forces were pulled to other theatres, though both have since pledged increases.

claims.text: The war in Ukraine has become a war of attrition [2024]
claims.note: SIPRI describes Russia's invasion as having 'gradually become a war of attrition', with Russia switching to high volumes of cheaper weapons.

claims.text: Great powers use military force to secure economic spheres of influence
claims.note: Some great powers have fought for economic spheres, as Japan did in 1941, but since 1945 most have sought economic influence through trade and investment rather than conquest.

claims.text: If Russia wins in Ukraine it will go on to attack other European countries
claims.note: DDIS makes the Ukraine war ending or freezing the first condition for a Russian attack on NATO, after which resources flow to the build-up; it is a condition for a threat, not a prediction of attack.

claims.text: Only a small minority of Western Europeans would fight to defend their country
claims.note: Surveys such as Gallup's 2024 poll found only about a quarter or fewer of Germans, Italians and others say they would fight for their country.

claims.text: Supporting Ukraine now costs Europe less than defending against Russia later
claims.note: Studies such as the Kiel Institute's put aid to Ukraine at a fraction of the cost of rearming against a victorious Russia, but the estimate rests on assuming Russia would attack.

claims.text: Ukraine retook more territory than Russia captured [2025]
claims.note: Open-source trackers such as ISW and DeepState show Russia gaining several thousand square kilometres in 2025 against small Ukrainian recaptures.

claims.text: China lacks the military capability to take Taiwan by force
claims.note: DDIS (Dec 2025): 'It is highly unlikely that China currently possesses the capability to launch a successful invasion', though it expects readiness to grow.

claims.text: Counting tanks, ships and troops misjudges military strength
claims.note: Quality, training, logistics and integration decide outcomes, as the 1991 Gulf War and Russia's 2022 performance showed against raw counts.

claims.text: The US spends more on its military than China and Russia combined
claims.note: SIPRI puts 2025 US spending at $954 billion against an estimated $336 billion for China and $190 billion for Russia ($526 billion combined), at market exchange rates.

claims.text: A world war needs rival blocs with rough military and economic parity
claims.note: Power-transition research links great wars to narrowing power gaps, but wars have also begun between unequal sides and the US lead over China has narrowed.

claims.text: Russia has failed to gain air superiority over Ukraine [2026]
claims.note: Ukrainian ground-based air defence has kept Russian aircraft largely to stand-off weapons such as glide bombs throughout the war.

claims.text: Iran's military cannot stand up to the US military
claims.note: In conventional terms Iran is vastly outmatched, though it can impose costs asymmetrically through missiles, drones and shipping attacks.

claims.text: Russia is rapidly scaling production of long-range strike drones and missiles
claims.note: DDIS reports long-range strikes rising sharply in 2025 with growing drone and missile production; its chart shows long-range drone output going from at least 500 in 2022 to at least 35,000 in 2025.

claims.text: Russia's air force has not closed its pre-war capability gaps
claims.note: Analysts such as RUSI find Russian air power still weak at suppressing air defences and at complex air operations, relying on stand-off strikes.

claims.text: The Russian military can absorb heavy losses and keep fighting a long war
claims.note: US intelligence says Russia's ground forces have grown even with wartime attrition and Moscow is confident it will prevail.

claims.text: Russia cannot sustain wartime defense spending for long after the war
claims.note: Deficits, rising debt and deferred civilian spending strain the budget, but states have sustained high military spending for years when they accept the trade-offs.

claims.text: Russia's military will shrink once wartime stop-loss is lifted
claims.note: Many contracts are held only by stop-loss and the force is old, but Moscow could raise conscription or pay to hold numbers.

claims.text: NATO militaries are not yet adapted to the drone and missile warfare seen in Ukraine
claims.note: Exercise reports and munitions-stock shortfalls point to gaps in counter-drone defence and mass missile defence, though NATO is adapting.

claims.text: European NATO defense spending has surged since 2022
claims.note: European spending rose 14 percent in 2025 to a record $864 billion and doubled over 2016-25; the 29 European NATO members spent $559 billion.

claims.text: Russia will fall behind a rearming Europe in the long-run military competition
claims.note: Europe's economy is many times Russia's, but turning money into forces is slow and Russia's war industry is already running.

claims.text: Wargames are analytical tools, not predictions of what will happen
claims.note: CSIS says its specific numbers 'are not intended to imply that these are precise predictions' but share the raw data behind its judgments, and elsewhere that modelling an invasion does not imply it is probable.

claims.text: Russia could not surprise NATO with an attack on the Baltic states
claims.note: A large build-up would be seen, but 2022 showed leaders may disbelieve warning, and a small snap attack would shorten it.

claims.text: Doubt about the US commitment to NATO raises the risk of a Russian attack
claims.note: DDIS says Russia's willingness to provoke and confront European NATO states would rise if the US publicly doubted it would respond or withdrew troops, and lists a perceived US unwillingness among the conditions for a Russian attack.

claims.text: NATO's Article 5 does not automatically oblige allies to fight
claims.note: The treaty commits each ally only to such action as it deems necessary, so a military response is a political choice.

claims.text: NATO cannot yet move forces to its eastern flank fast enough to deter Russia
claims.note: NATO and the EU acknowledge military-mobility gaps in permits, bridges and rail, though forward-deployed brigades reduce the need for speed.

claims.text: Russia is unable to make breakthroughs in Ukraine [2026]
claims.note: Russia has gained ground slowly through infiltration at heavy cost without any operational breakthrough since 2022.

claims.text: Putin has no interest in ending the war in Ukraine
claims.note: EFIS: the Kremlin 'merely feigns interest in peace talks' to buy time and has no intention of ending the war until its objectives are achieved or conditions are favourable.

claims.text: Military strikes can delay but not eliminate Iran's ability to build a bomb
claims.note: Knowledge and industrial base survive strikes, and the 2025 strikes set the program back without accounting for its enriched uranium.

claims.text: Iran still holds a stockpile of highly enriched uranium after the strikes [2026]
claims.note: After the 2026 strikes, Israel's condition for a final deal was that Iran relinquish its 60 per cent enriched nuclear material, implying Iran still held it.

claims.text: A nuclear-armed Iran could be managed through deterrence
claims.note: Deterrence has held with North Korea, but a nuclear Iran could spur regional proliferation and riskier crises.

claims.text: Nuclear weapons have not stopped nuclear-armed India and Pakistan from fighting
claims.note: Nuclear-armed India and Pakistan fought a brief armed conflict in May 2025, with India attacking Pakistani bases likely to have nuclear roles, though both sides took steps to avoid escalation.

claims.text: Periods of nuclear tension have historically eased within a few years
claims.note: The Cuban crisis was followed by the 1963 test ban and the 1983 war scare by the INF treaty, but some rivalries stayed tense for decades.

claims.text: Nuclear weapons technology is old enough that any industrial state can build it
claims.note: The physics and engineering are well known, but producing fissile material in secret remains the main barrier, which is why few states have succeeded.

claims.text: A renewed war with Iran would collapse the global economy
claims.note: A Gulf supply shock can push oil far higher and cause recession, but a collapse worse than the 1930s goes well beyond what the 2026 disruption produced.

claims.text: The Gulf monarchies would collapse in a renewed war with Iran
claims.note: The Gulf monarchies have survived repeated Iranian and Houthi attacks on their infrastructure, and their reserves and security services are large.

claims.text: Iran, Russia and China are drawing closer into a bloc against the US
claims.note: US intelligence expects the four to keep seeking more cooperation, but says divergent interests and fear of confronting the US will limit it, short of a bloc.

claims.text: The US keeps a launch-on-warning posture that gives the president minutes to decide
claims.note: The US keeps ICBMs ready to launch under attack and decision times of minutes are widely cited, though official policy says it does not rely on launch on warning.

claims.text: The risk of nuclear war is higher now than during the Cold War
claims.note: The Doomsday Clock is at its closest ever and arms control has lapsed, but forecasters do not rate today's risk above the Cold War's worst crises.

claims.text: An ICBM cannot be recalled once launched
claims.note: US ICBMs have no recall or self-destruct mechanism after launch.

claims.text: Iran lacks the missiles to strike the United States
claims.note: US intelligence says that before the 2026 war Iran had only space-launch vehicles it could turn into a military ICBM by 2035 if it chose to, so it had no missile able to reach the US.

claims.text: A large share of the world's oil and gas exports passes through the Strait of Hormuz
claims.note: The EIA puts about a fifth of world petroleum liquids and a similar share of LNG trade through the strait.

claims.text: The US is largely shielded from a Gulf oil shock because it produces its own oil
claims.note: US production protects supply, but oil is priced globally, so US fuel prices still rise with a Gulf disruption.

claims.text: The US and China will go to war over Taiwan in 2025
claims.note: UCDP's list of every state-based armed conflict active in 2025 includes no conflict between China and the US or over Taiwan.

claims.text: Putin seeks to recreate the Russian Empire
claims.note: DDIS says the Putin regime sees extensive control over the former Soviet space (Ukraine, Belarus, Moldova, Georgia) as a prerequisite for great-power status: control, not necessarily annexation of an empire.

claims.text: The risk of a great-power war is higher now than at any time since the end of the Cold War
claims.note: Threat assessments, the Doomsday Clock and forecasters agree that Russia-West risk is higher than at any point since 1991, though still unlikely in any year.

claims.text: Russian drones or missiles are likely to hit NATO territory in incidents Russia calls accidents
claims.note: Russian drones repeatedly entered Polish, Romanian and Baltic airspace in 2025, with Moscow denying intent.

claims.text: Russia aims to show that NATO will not defend its members
claims.note: DDIS assesses Russia's hybrid attacks aim to undermine NATO cohesion and that provocations could test whether the US would actually come to Europe's aid.

claims.text: AI speeds up warfare so that humans lose control of escalation
claims.note: SIPRI concludes AI's capacity to introduce errors, amplify automation bias and shorten decision timelines raises the risk of inadvertent nuclear escalation (the UK warns of 'machine-speed escalation'), a risk assessment rather than evidence that humans have lost control.

claims.text: Warfare too fast for human control is still decades away
claims.note: Writing in 2021, CNAS judged that militaries were only beginning to adopt AI and that near-term use would be limited and incremental, with profound change only over time; that supports 'not imminent' but gives no timescale of decades and predates recent battlefield use.

claims.text: Humans must keep control of every decision to use nuclear weapons
claims.note: In November 2024 Biden and Xi affirmed the need to maintain human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons, the stated position of both leaders (US readout); a norm, not a testable fact.

claims.text: AI could undermine nuclear deterrence by making hidden forces easier to find
claims.note: SIPRI cites a 2024 Lawrence Livermore report that AI-enhanced anti-submarine warfare threatens the survivability of US missile submarines, and Chinese analysts who fear AI tracking of mobile launchers will threaten their retaliatory forces.

claims.text: AI could make war less likely by improving warning and reducing miscalculation
claims.note: RAND says AI could enable more reliable early warning and reduce accidental escalation, but calls it a mixed blessing that needs fortuitous conditions: equal access, benign intentions and justified confidence.

claims.text: The US and China are in an AI arms race
claims.note: They compete hard over AI and chips, but military AI spending is a small share of budgets and China is not visibly racing for AGI, so 'arms race' overstates it.

claims.text: AI-enabled cyberattacks could cripple a country's infrastructure in a war
claims.note: Infrastructure software is often old and exposed, but past attacks such as those on Ukraine's grid caused short outages rather than crippling a country.

claims.text: AI could cause a global catastrophe this century
claims.note: In the 2022 XPT tournament the median superforecaster put the risk of an AI-caused catastrophe (over 10% of humans dead) by 2100 at 2.13% and the median AI expert at 12%: both groups see it as possible, at low to moderate odds.

claims.text: Putting AI into nuclear command and control raises the risk of nuclear war
claims.note: Most experts judge that automating warning or decision support adds error and speed risks, but no state has disclosed deep integration and the effect is unmeasured.

claims.text: AI tools are already used across nuclear command, control and communications systems
claims.note: Automation and signal processing are long established in US early warning and NC3, but how much modern machine learning is used is not public.

claims.text: AI systems fail unpredictably in situations outside their training data
claims.note: CNAS notes that AI trained on inadequate data or used outside its design context is often brittle, performing well in the lab and failing dramatically when conditions change, as with self-driving cars.

claims.text: Adversaries can fool or poison military AI systems
claims.note: RAND cites numerous demonstrations that small adversarial efforts subvert machine learning with outsized effect, and describes hacking, training-data poisoning and input manipulation that works even without access to the system.

claims.text: Operators over-trust automated systems, so a human in the loop does not guarantee control
claims.note: Automation bias is well documented, including the 2003 Patriot fratricides and driver-assist crashes.

claims.text: The US and China agreed in 2024 to keep human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons
claims.note: The White House readout of the 16 November 2024 Lima meeting states the two leaders affirmed the need to maintain human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons; this is the US account, China published its own separately.

claims.text: China is not racing the US to build artificial general intelligence
claims.note: Beijing's intentions are not public; its stated priorities stress applications and diffusion, but a covert programme cannot be ruled out.

claims.text: China would invade Taiwan to seize its chip factories if it fell far behind in AI
claims.note: A statement about Chinese leaders' intentions that no public record can show.

claims.text: The race mentality in AI is pushing the US to drop safety guardrails
claims.note: The Bulletin says the US administration, rushing to apply AI, revoked the previous executive order on AI safety, a prioritization of AI innovation over safety that is mirrored in other major powers.

claims.text: Chinese AI models trail the best American models by only months
claims.note: Benchmark trackers such as Epoch AI and Artificial Analysis estimate the gap at months rather than years.

claims.text: US chip export controls slow China's AI in the near term but speed up its own chip industry
claims.note: Controls have limited China's access to top chips while Beijing has poured money into domestic alternatives such as Huawei's Ascend.

claims.text: Frontier AI models raise the risk of damaging cyberattacks and bioweapons
claims.note: AI labs and government evaluators report growing cyber-offence and bio-uplift capabilities in frontier models, though real-world harm so far is limited.

claims.text: An arms-control treaty on AI between the US and China is not feasible yet
claims.note: Low trust and the difficulty of verifying software make binding AI limits unlikely now; talks so far are limited to dialogue.

claims.text: Mass-produced autonomous weapons would deter China from invading Taiwan
claims.note: Untested; deterrence depends on many factors and autonomous mass has not been fielded at scale in the Pacific.

claims.text: Taiwan makes nearly all of the world's most advanced chips
claims.note: TSMC produces roughly nine in ten of the world's leading-edge logic chips.

claims.text: Fully autonomous weapons that choose their own targets are already in use
claims.note: Loitering munitions and air defences have autonomous modes, but documented use with no human target approval is rare and disputed.

claims.text: Countries go to war only when they disagree about who would win
claims.note: Disagreement about relative power is one recognised cause of war, but commitment problems and indivisible stakes also cause wars, so 'only' is too strong.

claims.text: AI weapons reduce civilian casualties by making strikes more precise
claims.note: Precision weapons have cut collateral damage compared with area bombing, but AI targeting has not been shown to reduce civilian harm and may speed up strikes.

claims.text: A country close to decisive AI superiority could be attacked preventively by its rival
claims.note: SIPRI says technological imbalance can make a weaker nuclear state doubt its second strike and tempt it to strike first, which fits the mechanism for AI-enabled counterforce rather than decisive AI superiority in general.

claims.text: The US-China race for AI supremacy could lead to war
claims.note: Analysts widely flag the AI race as a source of tension, but it has so far stayed economic and technological, and forecasters see no near-term war driven by it.

claims.text: Threats of mutual sabotage could deter states from racing to build superintelligence
claims.note: This is the paper's central MAIM thesis: because a rival's AI project is easy to sabotage, states must expect any bid for monopoly to be maimed, giving deterrence without treaties; an untested proposal by its advocates.

claims.text: The current AI arms race resembles the nuclear arms race
claims.note: AI shares dual-use and proliferation features with nuclear technology, but it is diffuse, commercially driven and has no single destructive threshold like a bomb.

claims.text: Cutting-edge AI chips are harder for a state to produce than nuclear weapons
claims.note: Leading-edge chipmaking depends on a few firms and tools no state replicates alone, while several poor states have built bombs, though the cost comparison is rough.

claims.text: Export controls on advanced chips can keep frontier AI away from rogue states
claims.note: Controls raise costs and slow access, but chip smuggling and cloud access have repeatedly leaked advanced chips to restricted buyers.

claims.text: A war over Taiwan would cut the US off from advanced chips
claims.note: Taiwan makes the large majority of the most advanced logic chips, and new US fabs cover only a small share of that capacity so far.

claims.text: Jamming pushes militaries to make drones autonomous
claims.note: In Ukraine heavy jamming has driven both sides toward terminal autonomy and fibre-optic drones.

claims.text: Fully automated AI research would carry a high risk of losing control of AI
claims.note: WEF says the more AI agents are used in R&D to develop AI, the greater the risk their developers cease to understand how the systems work, and the harder governance becomes; it names a risk without calling it high.

claims.text: Competitive pressure will push societies to hand more and more decisions to AI
claims.note: Firms and militaries are adopting AI for competitive reasons, but how far decision authority will be handed over is still uncertain.

claims.text: A rising power becomes most dangerous once it believes it has become strong
claims.note: Power-transition theory supports the idea, but historians dispute how often rising powers start wars rather than declining ones.

claims.text: China has become more willing to risk escalation as its power has grown
claims.note: The evidence offered is war-game impressions; Beijing's real risk tolerance in a crisis is not publicly knowable.

claims.text: Different US and Chinese views of what AI can do raise the risk of misperception in a crisis
claims.note: RAND stresses that AI's strategic effect depends as much on adversaries' perceptions as on real capability: a tracking system need only be perceived as capable to be destabilizing.

claims.text: China is producing more AI researchers than the United States
claims.note: China graduates more STEM students and produces more top AI papers and undergraduate-trained AI researchers than the US, though many top researchers still work in the US.

claims.text: Autonomous drones and drone swarms are transforming warfare
claims.note: Estonian intelligence reports Ukraine's commander saying drones cause up to 70% of equipment losses and Russia building a dedicated unmanned systems branch, which shows drones transforming warfare, but it describes mass-produced unmanned systems, not autonomy or swarms.

claims.text: China's advanced chipmaking lags the US and its allies by several years
claims.note: Without EUV tools China's leading node trails TSMC by several years and yields are lower, though the gap estimate varies.

claims.text: Semiconductors would not be the main reason for a US-China war over Taiwan
claims.note: A judgment about the motives of a war that has not happened.

claims.text: AI language models tend to escalate toward nuclear use in simulated crises
claims.note: Several war-game studies of current models found escalation bias and frequent nuclear use, though simulations differ from real command systems.

claims.text: AI models hallucinate too often to be trusted with nuclear decisions
claims.note: Current language models still produce confident false outputs at rates no nuclear decision system could accept.

claims.text: Announcing AI in nuclear command and control raises public perceptions of deterrence
claims.note: The evidence is a few survey experiments by one research group; it has not been widely replicated.

claims.text: Russia's nuclear modernization has stalled
claims.note: SIPRI says Russia's nuclear modernization is facing challenges (another failed Sarmat test in 2025, sanctions and war demands) but also reports a claimed successful Burevestnik test and a new Oreshnik base in Belarus, so troubled rather than stalled.

claims.text: The UN General Assembly has called for human control over AI in nuclear command and control
claims.note: The panel's diplomat co-authored the 2025 resolution; its exact wording on human control varied during negotiation.

claims.text: The US military uses AI to find and rank targets in its current wars
claims.note: Maven Smart System is in wide use for target identification and prioritization, as officials have described publicly.

claims.text: Militaries are removing humans from parts of the targeting decision cycle
claims.note: US demonstrations and Israeli practice show human steps cut or reduced to supervision, though final strike approval formally stays with humans.

claims.text: AI targeting can make errors faster and at greater scale than humans
claims.note: Automated systems can repeat an error across many targets quickly, but comparative error rates against human targeting are not public.

claims.text: The US military is ahead of China in adopting AI for war
claims.note: Neither side publishes its assessment, and China's military AI adoption is opaque.

claims.text: Military AI could increase harm to civilians rather than reduce it
claims.note: SIPRI reports Chinese experts' concern that AI could increase collateral damage among other risks, an expert opinion not backed by data here.

claims.text: AI could launch nuclear weapons without a human decision
claims.note: CNAS notes the Soviet Perimeter system reportedly had semiautomated 'dead hand' functionality and that some states may want automated retaliation, while the US says no and no state is known to deploy an uninhabited nuclear launch platform; possible in principle, not shown in use.

claims.text: AI models do not grasp the stakes of nuclear war as humans do
claims.note: CNAS says even the most advanced AI cannot understand broad guidance such as 'defend our claims, but don't start a war' or show human common sense, which bears on grasping context, not on nuclear stakes as such (and predates large language models).

claims.text: Over-reliance on AI advice could lead commanders into mistaken nuclear decisions
claims.note: Automation bias is well documented in military and civilian settings, though its effect on nuclear decisions is untested.

claims.text: Adversaries could manipulate the data feeding military AI to sway nuclear decisions
claims.note: RAND warns an adversary could manipulate an AI's inputs, for example by mobilizing forces in a set pattern, so that it judges an incoming strike safe, and that such attacks do not need access to the system.

claims.text: A rogue AI agent could provoke a nuclear crisis by fabricating intelligence or spoofing communications
claims.note: WEF says weaponized generative AI can fabricate executive orders or convincing battlefield footage that confuses humans and automated responses; that supports fabrication as a crisis risk but not a rogue agent or a nuclear crisis specifically.

claims.text: Drones will soon fight and choose targets fully autonomously without human involvement
claims.note: Autonomy is spreading fast in Ukraine, but most strike drones still need a human to pick the target and full autonomy at scale is not imminent.

claims.text: Today's arms race is the most destructive in human history because it includes AI
claims.note: The Cold War nuclear build-up to tens of thousands of warheads remains far more destructive than any AI arms race so far.

commonlyWrong.text: World War 3 has already started
commonlyWrong.note: No direct war between great powers is under way; the wars in Ukraine and with Iran remain regional.

commonlyWrong.text: The US and China are headed for war
commonlyWrong.note: Metaculus's 629 forecasters put a US-China war (1,000 battle deaths in a year) at 8.7% before 2035; linked questions put it at 25% before 2050 and 0.5% by 2027.

commonlyWrong.text: A limited nuclear exchange would escalate to all-out nuclear war
commonlyWrong.note: FRI participants said a deliberate non-test detonation before 2030 would raise their probability of a 10-million-death catastrophe by 2045 4x (experts, from 5%) or 6.7x (superforecasters, from 1%), well short of certain escalation.

commonlyWrong.text: The current conflicts are linked into one global war between two blocs
commonlyWrong.note: The wars share some backers, such as Iranian drones and North Korean troops for Russia, but they are not one coordinated war, and China and Russia stayed out of the Iran war.

commonlyWrong.text: A direct war between great powers is likely within the next few years
commonlyWrong.note: Metaculus's 'World War Three before 2050?' stands at 22% over about 24 years (3.3k forecasters), and the question conditional on AGI arriving puts World War III within five years of AGI at 4% (66 forecasters), both far under even odds for the next few years.

commonlyWrong.text: The US probably could not defeat China in a war over Taiwan
commonlyWrong.note: CSIS's wargame found the US and Taiwan 'could successfully defend the island even under relatively pessimistic assumptions', contrary to many observers' impressions, though only if four conditions hold.

commonlyWrong.text: Putin did not intend to conquer all of Ukraine
commonlyWrong.note: RAND describes Russia's 'expansive goals at the outset', including capturing Kyiv and 'denazifying' the government, scaled back to annexing four provinces only after failure.

commonlyWrong.text: The American empire will collapse within the next decade
commonlyWrong.note: No base rate or model supports a dated collapse; the US remains the largest military and the issuer of the main reserve currency.

commonlyWrong.text: The US attacked Iran to defend the dollar's reserve-currency status
commonlyWrong.note: The paper gives the war's aims as subduing Iran or toppling its regime and does not mention the dollar.

commonlyWrong.text: If attacked, Iran would strike Gulf oil production rather than close the Strait of Hormuz
commonlyWrong.note: When attacked in 2026, Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, and reopening it became the US condition for a truce.

commonlyWrong.text: Britain faces an imminent all-out war
commonlyWrong.note: The army chief urged preparation, not a date; forecasters put a direct NATO-Russia war within a few years well under even odds.

commonlyWrong.text: The US cannot survive a global conflict if Russia and China are aligned against it
commonlyWrong.note: The US and its allies outweigh Russia and China in economic output and naval power; the claim is a sweeping assertion.

commonlyWrong.text: China's economy would be half again larger than the US economy by 2024
commonlyWrong.note: US nominal GDP was $10 trillion larger than China's in 2024, and at 2025 growth rates China would not pass the US in nominal GDP until 2041.

commonlyWrong.text: China's military budget has grown faster than its economy for years
commonlyWrong.note: China's estimated spending has risen 31 years running (62 percent over 2016-25) but held at 1.7 percent of GDP in 2025, the same as its 2016-24 average, so it has grown roughly in line with the economy, not faster.

commonlyWrong.text: The US and China will go to war over Taiwan in 2025
commonlyWrong.note: UCDP's list of every state-based armed conflict active in 2025 includes no conflict between China and the US or over Taiwan.

commonlyWrong.text: Chinese covert influence turned Taiwan's parliament pro-unification [2024]
commonlyWrong.note: The opposition majority came from Taiwan's 2024 election; the KMT favours engagement with Beijing, not unification, and support for unification in Taiwan remains small.

commonlyWrong.text: Conflict will break out in East Asia while the US is tied down in the Middle East
commonlyWrong.note: No forecast or official threat assessment puts a war over Taiwan, Korea or the South China Sea in the next few years at anything near even odds.

commonlyWrong.text: Control of the Strait of Hormuz will make Iran a fourth centre of world power
commonlyWrong.note: Iran's economy is a small fraction of the US, Chinese or Indian economy and transit leverage does not create industrial or military power on that scale.

commonlyWrong.text: Countries go to war only when they disagree about who would win
commonlyWrong.note: Disagreement about relative power is one recognised cause of war, but commitment problems and indivisible stakes also cause wars, so 'only' is too strong.

commonlyWrong.text: The US faces a serious risk of civil war within the next decade
commonlyWrong.note: Polarisation and political violence are rising, but forecasters and scholars put an organised US civil war far below one in three.

commonlyWrong.text: France is deploying its nuclear warheads across Europe as a shield against Russia [2024]
commonlyWrong.note: In 2024 Macron only offered to discuss a European dimension of French deterrence; he did not move submarine warheads across Europe.

commonlyWrong.text: Governments would hide a successful interception of a nuclear missile
commonlyWrong.note: There is no evidence any nuclear-armed missile has been fired at a state, and a launch would be seen by many countries' early-warning satellites.

commonlyWrong.text: Great powers are locked in security competition that cannot be escaped
commonlyWrong.note: Hanania quotes Mearsheimer and Walt on unavoidable competition (L101-114) but answers that great-power antagonism is a choice made by both sides, not 'the result of circumstances outside of human control'. Both positions are argued, not demonstrated.

commonlyWrong.text: The Gulf monarchies would collapse in a renewed war with Iran
commonlyWrong.note: The Gulf monarchies have survived repeated Iranian and Houthi attacks on their infrastructure, and their reserves and security services are large.

commonlyWrong.text: Iran is more likely than not to get a nuclear weapon within a year
commonlyWrong.note: FRI's 2024 experts and superforecasters gave Iran 25% and 30% chances of acquiring nuclear weapons by 2030, so not more likely than not within a year.

commonlyWrong.text: Iran is the most powerful opponent the US has fought since the Second World War
commonlyWrong.note: The US fought China directly in the Korean War, a far larger military, and Iran's economy and conventional forces are much smaller than a great power's.

commonlyWrong.text: Iran will drive the US military out of the Middle East
commonlyWrong.note: US forces stayed in the Gulf through 2026, with more carrier groups sent in, and no withdrawal has been announced.

commonlyWrong.text: Iran will have a nuclear weapon within a year if the US ends the 2026 war
commonlyWrong.note: Strikes in 2025 and 2026 destroyed much of Iran's enrichment and weapons infrastructure; a bomb within a year is possible but not the expected case.

commonlyWrong.text: Israel, not the US president, is directing US war policy on Iran
commonlyWrong.note: Trump set and extended the deadlines and accepted a ceasefire to which Israel was not a party, while Israel claimed it would comply with whatever Washington asked.

commonlyWrong.text: The US-Israeli war on Iran is aimed at weakening Russia and China
commonlyWrong.note: The paper gives the war's aims as subduing Iran or toppling its regime and does not mention weakening Russia or China.

commonlyWrong.text: The US no longer keeps tactical nuclear weapons in its arsenal
commonlyWrong.note: The US still holds B61 gravity bombs, about a hundred of them deployed in Europe, and fielded the low-yield W76-2 warhead in 2020.

commonlyWrong.text: Missile defences would intercept a nuclear missile attack
commonlyWrong.note: Missile defences are tested against a few missiles, succeed about half the time and cannot stop a large attack.

commonlyWrong.text: NATO is finished [2026]
commonlyWrong.note: NATO still functions: all 32 members met at the 2026 summit and Article 5 stands, though US commitment has weakened.

commonlyWrong.text: NATO and Russia will fight directly over Odessa
commonlyWrong.note: NATO governments have repeatedly ruled out sending combat forces to fight Russia in Ukraine, and forecasters put a direct NATO-Russia war well under even odds.

commonlyWrong.text: Nostradamus accurately predicted Napoleon and Hitler
commonlyWrong.note: 'Hister' is the Latin name of the Danube and the Napoleon anagram needs letter swaps; the matches were fitted after the events.

commonlyWrong.text: Nostradamus predicted a third world war
commonlyWrong.note: The quatrains are vague verse read after the fact; none names a third world war, its date or its parties, and no reading has forecast a war before it happened.

commonlyWrong.text: A nuclear-armed state facing defeat would use its nuclear weapons before losing
commonlyWrong.note: Nuclear powers have lost or retreated without using them (the US in Vietnam, the Soviets in Afghanistan, Israel's early 1973 setbacks, Russia in 2022).

commonlyWrong.text: President Trump could be removed from office over the Iran war
commonlyWrong.note: Removal needs two-thirds of the Senate and no US president has ever been removed; the base rate is near zero.

commonlyWrong.text: Psychic visions can predict when a world war will start
commonlyWrong.note: Tests of psychic forecasting find no accuracy above chance, and this source's own timing for the war has already shifted.

commonlyWrong.text: The US is raising its defence budget because it expects a major war
commonlyWrong.note: SIPRI finds US military spending fell 7.5 percent in 2025 to $954 billion, mainly because supplemental aid to Ukraine stopped; its stated priorities are nuclear modernization and deterring China, not preparing for an expected major war.

commonlyWrong.text: A renewed war with Iran would collapse the global economy
commonlyWrong.note: A Gulf supply shock can push oil far higher and cause recession, but a collapse worse than the 1930s goes well beyond what the 2026 disruption produced.

commonlyWrong.text: Rising gold and silver prices show investors expect a major war
commonlyWrong.note: Precious metals rose on central-bank buying, interest rates and currency worries; prices do not single out war.

commonlyWrong.text: Russia and China have formed a military alliance
commonlyWrong.note: DoD 2025: despite deeper ties, Beijing and Moscow 'remain unwilling to establish a formal defense alliance with mutual security guarantees', still distrust each other, and China has withheld lethal aid for Russia's war.

commonlyWrong.text: Russia, China, Iran and Turkey are forming an axis that will dominate the Middle East
commonlyWrong.note: Turkey is a NATO member at odds with Iran and Russia in Syria, and the others cooperate loosely without any alliance.

commonlyWrong.text: Russia complied with the nuclear arms treaties the US abandoned
commonlyWrong.note: US intelligence says Russia has undermined arms-control agreements, suspended required New START data exchanges and deratified the CTBT, contradicting a record of compliance.

commonlyWrong.text: Russia and Iran will lead a coalition invasion of Israel
commonlyWrong.note: Russia keeps working ties with Israel and has shown no intent to attack it; Iran's strikes have been missile and proxy attacks, not an invasion with Russia.

commonlyWrong.text: Russia never negotiates an end to a war unless it has already won or lost
commonlyWrong.note: Russia has accepted negotiated stalemates, such as the 1996 Khasavyurt accord in Chechnya and the 1940 Moscow Peace that ended the Winter War short of its aims.

commonlyWrong.text: Russia will attack a NATO country within the next few years
commonlyWrong.note: Estonia's foreign intelligence (Feb 2026) assesses Russia has no intention of attacking Estonia or any NATO member in the coming year and expects the same next year, while warning capabilities will grow.

commonlyWrong.text: Russia will not stop until it reaches the Danube, the Carpathians, the Vistula and the Baltic
commonlyWrong.note: That line runs through NATO territory, and forecasters put a Russian attack on NATO well under even odds; Russia's stated war aims centre on Ukraine.

commonlyWrong.text: Sanctions on Russia have had no effect
commonlyWrong.note: DDIS: Western sanctions exert intense pressure on Russia's economy, are a major factor in its reduced energy earnings, and have made military components more costly to obtain.

commonlyWrong.text: The Saudi government will be overthrown within the next two years
commonlyWrong.note: The Saudi monarchy has a long record of stability and there is no sign of an imminent revolt.

commonlyWrong.text: Taiwan will come under China's control peacefully as their economies grow together
commonlyWrong.note: Polls in Taiwan show support for unification in single digits and a rising Taiwanese identity, so peaceful absorption looks unlikely on current trends.

commonlyWrong.text: A third world war is inevitable
commonlyWrong.note: The Metaculus community gives a third world war only a 22% chance before 2050, the opposite of inevitable over the next quarter-century.

commonlyWrong.text: A third world war would be short
commonlyWrong.note: CSIS warns a US-China war 'might not end after this initial phase but drag on for months or even years', since opening battles, even seemingly decisive ones, rarely end a war.

commonlyWrong.text: Today's arms race is the most destructive in human history because it includes AI
commonlyWrong.note: The Cold War nuclear build-up to tens of thousands of warheads remains far more destructive than any AI arms race so far.

commonlyWrong.text: Ukraine retook more territory than Russia captured [2025]
commonlyWrong.note: Open-source trackers such as ISW and DeepState show Russia gaining several thousand square kilometres in 2025 against small Ukrainian recaptures.

commonlyWrong.text: The United States will reinstate a military draft because of the war with Iran
commonlyWrong.note: Automatic Selective Service registration is not a draft; induction needs a new act of Congress, and none has been proposed.

commonlyWrong.text: Using the Iran war to choke China's oil supply would lead to war with China
commonlyWrong.note: China has supplied Iran but avoided any military clash with the US during the war, and forecasters see a US-China war as unlikely in the near term.

commonlyWrong.text: The war with Iran will almost certainly escalate into a third world war
commonlyWrong.note: The 2026 war ended in a Pakistan-brokered ceasefire after about forty days with no great-power fighting; Russia and China only vetoed a UN resolution.

commonlyWrong.text: The war in Ukraine will spread to draw in Poland and Belarus
commonlyWrong.note: After more than four years neither Poland nor Belarus has joined the fighting despite drone incursions, and forecasters put a direct Russia-NATO war in the next few years well under even odds.

commonlyWrong.text: Western economies will collapse under the energy shock of the war with Iran
commonlyWrong.note: Past oil shocks caused recessions, not collapse, and benchmark prices eased during the war.

commonlyWrong.text: The US will invade Cuba within the next few years
commonlyWrong.note: Pressure, sanctions and an oil blockade are not an invasion, and nothing in the public record points to a planned invasion.

commonlyWrong.text: The world is closer to a third world war than ever before
commonlyWrong.note: Forecasters put great-power war well below even odds, and the Cuban missile crisis and 1983 were closer calls than anything on record since.

commonlyWrong.text: World War 3 will start in 2028
commonlyWrong.note: Metaculus forecasters give a world war 22% over the whole 2019-2050 window, so a start in the single year 2028 is far less likely than not.

commonlyWrong.text: World War 3 will be triggered by false-flag attacks staged by globalists
commonlyWrong.note: There is no evidence of any plan to stage false flags to start a world war; the claim rests on channelled visions.

commonlyWrong.text: China will invade Taiwan by 2027
commonlyWrong.note: The US intelligence community assesses that Chinese leaders do not currently plan to invade Taiwan in 2027 and have no fixed timeline for unification.

claim.text: A new nuclear arms race is beginning between the US, Russia and China
claim.note: SIPRI says the post-Cold War decline in warhead numbers is likely to reverse as dismantlement slows and deployment of new weapons accelerates, with states 'fuelling arms-race dynamics'.

priorRecord.note: All three are modernizing and China is expanding fast, but US and Russian deployed numbers have not yet grown much past the old treaty limits.

evidenceRecord.note: SIPRI says the post-Cold War decline in warhead numbers is likely to reverse as dismantlement slows and deployment of new weapons accelerates, with states 'fuelling arms-race dynamics'.

claim.text: US missile defences drive Russia and China to build up their nuclear forces
claim.note: Both cite US missile defence to justify new systems, but each also has other motives for its build-up.

priorRecord.note: Both cite US missile defence to justify new systems, but each also has other motives for its build-up.

evidenceRecord.note: The Bulletin says missile defence systems are at best partially effective and serve as a provocation for the other side to invest in greater offensive capability; expert assessment, not a measured response.

claim.text: A full US-Russia nuclear exchange could cause a nuclear winter
claim.note: Climate models disagree on how much soot burning cities would loft; severe cooling is plausible but its size is disputed.

priorRecord.note: Climate models disagree on how much soot burning cities would loft; severe cooling is plausible but its size is disputed.

evidenceRecord.note: The introduction, citing Robock et al.'s nuclear-winter modelling, says a war using large fractions of the US and Russian arsenals could severely reduce food production for years; this is background, not the paper's own finding.

claim.text: A war with Iran would close the Strait of Hormuz and send oil prices soaring
claim.note: In the 2026 war Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, raising energy prices and creating what the paper calls an unprecedented global energy crisis.

priorRecord.note: Reports from the 2026 war describe Gulf shipping largely halted and oil near $100, but closure was partial and contested and the price effect depends on how long it lasts.

evidenceRecord.note: In the 2026 war Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, raising energy prices and creating what the paper calls an unprecedented global energy crisis.

claim.text: Air strikes alone cannot bring about regime change
claim.note: Studies of coercive air power find bombing rarely topples a regime without ground forces or an internal uprising.

priorRecord.note: Studies of coercive air power find bombing rarely topples a regime without ground forces or an internal uprising.

evidenceRecord.note: The 2026 US-Israeli air campaign meant to topple Iran's regime produced the opposite effect after six weeks; a single case that supports the claim.

claim.text: The US war with Iran is stuck in a stalemate [2026]
claim.note: By April 2026 the war had reached political deadlock, both sides claimed victory and the ceasefire came with no agreement on any US or Iranian point, but it ended in a truce rather than a static war.

priorRecord.note: Two former NSC Iran directors and the host describe a stalemate in October 2026; this is not independently verified here.

evidenceRecord.note: By April 2026 the war had reached political deadlock, both sides claimed victory and the ceasefire came with no agreement on any US or Iranian point, but it ended in a truce rather than a static war.

claim.text: China keeps Iran's economy afloat by buying its oil despite US sanctions
claim.note: Tanker-tracking estimates put China's share of Iran's exported oil at around 90 percent, bought through intermediaries.

priorRecord.note: Tanker-tracking estimates put China's share of Iran's exported oil at around 90 percent, bought through intermediaries.

evidenceRecord.note: US intelligence says China's economic support and growing trade have helped Tehran withstand US-led sanctions; oil purchases are not named here.

claim.text: US bases in the Gulf have become targets that expose host countries to attack
claim.note: Iran struck Al Udeid in 2025, and 2026 sources report Gulf bases and hosts hit again.

priorRecord.note: Iran struck Al Udeid in 2025, and 2026 sources report Gulf bases and hosts hit again.

evidenceRecord.note: During the 2026 war Iraqi Shia militias answered Iran's call to attack US bases, causing some damage; the assessment shows bases as targets but says little about attacks on host countries.

claim.text: The world is closer to a third world war than ever before
claim.note: Forecasters put great-power war well below even odds, and the Cuban missile crisis and 1983 were closer calls than anything on record since.

priorRecord.note: Forecasters put great-power war well below even odds, and the Cuban missile crisis and 1983 were closer calls than anything on record since.

evidenceRecord.note: The Clock is at its closest-ever setting, but it measures global catastrophe from several technologies (including climate and biology), not the odds of a world war, so 'closest ever' does not transfer directly to world war.

claim.text: The US and China are in a second Cold War
claim.note: A common and useful analogy for the rivalry since about 2018, but the two economies are far more entwined than the US and Soviet ones were.

priorRecord.note: A common and useful analogy for the rivalry since about 2018, but the two economies are far more entwined than the US and Soviet ones were.

evidenceRecord.note: Eurasia Group's 2026 outlook says there is not (yet) a second Cold War, with China remaking the global system and the US and allies resisting.

claim.text: Drones have made the war in Ukraine exceptionally lethal
claim.note: Ukrainian and Western estimates attribute most battlefield casualties on both sides to drones.

priorRecord.note: Ukrainian and Western estimates attribute most battlefield casualties on both sides to drones.

evidenceRecord.note: EFIS cites Ukraine's commander-in-chief that drones cause up to 70% of losses of weapons and equipment, which shows drones dominate attrition but not whether the war is unusually deadly overall.

claim.text: North Korean missiles can reach the continental United States
claim.note: US intelligence states North Korea has successfully tested ICBMs capable of reaching the entire US homeland.

priorRecord.note: Hwasong-15 and later tests show ICBM range, but reliable re-entry of a warhead has not been demonstrated.

evidenceRecord.note: US intelligence states North Korea has successfully tested ICBMs capable of reaching the entire US homeland.

claim.text: Russia has moved to a war economy that is producing tanks at a high rate [2026]
claim.note: Russian defence spending is around 6-7 percent of GDP and open-source counts show large refurbishment and new T-90M output.

priorRecord.note: Russian defence spending is around 6-7 percent of GDP and open-source counts show large refurbishment and new T-90M output.

evidenceRecord.note: DDIS says Russia's defence industry has produced more equipment and ammunition than the war consumes since 2024 and out-produces Europe's, but gives no tank figures and expects output hard to raise beyond 2025 levels.

claim.text: World War 3 is much less likely than social media makes it seem
claim.note: Forecasters put great-power war in the next few years well below even odds, while feeds amplify alarming content.

priorRecord.note: Forecasters put great-power war in the next few years well below even odds, while feeds amplify alarming content.

evidenceRecord.note: The US public's median forecast of a 10-million-death nuclear catastrophe by 2045 was 10%, against 5% for experts and 1% for superforecasters, so public perception runs above expert forecasts; social media itself is not measured.

claim.text: Great-power war has become rare since 1945 and remains unlikely in any given year
claim.note: Clauset: a constant-hazard model gives about a 43% chance of a WWII-sized war per century, small in any one year, but the long peace since 1945 is not statistically distinguishable from chance, so the 'has become rare' part is not shown.

priorRecord.note: Apart from US-Chinese fighting in Korea, no great powers have fought each other directly since 1945, and forecasters put the yearly chance in low single digits.

evidenceRecord.note: Clauset: a constant-hazard model gives about a 43% chance of a WWII-sized war per century, small in any one year, but the long peace since 1945 is not statistically distinguishable from chance, so the 'has become rare' part is not shown.

claim.text: The coming conflicts will be regional wars rather than one global war
claim.note: Conflict data show regional wars multiplying while forecasters keep a direct great-power war well below even odds in any given year, though this is a forecast.

priorRecord.note: Conflict data show regional wars multiplying while forecasters keep a direct great-power war well below even odds in any given year, though this is a forecast.

evidenceRecord.note: PRIO: today's interstate conflicts are border disputes, invasions and a Middle East regional escalation that could become a larger regional war, which fits the claim for now but says nothing of the future.

claim.text: Russia lacks the military capacity to fight NATO
claim.note: Russia's conventional forces are far weaker than NATO's combined, but it could mount a limited attack on a frontline state and holds a large nuclear arsenal.

priorRecord.note: Russia's conventional forces are far weaker than NATO's combined, but it could mount a limited attack on a frontline state and holds a large nuclear arsenal.

evidenceRecord.note: US intelligence calls Russia's robust conventional and nuclear forces an enduring threat to US allies, with ground forces grown and air and naval forces intact.

claim.text: Nuclear weapons will not be used in today's wars
claim.note: US intelligence judges Russia will probably keep abiding by the norm against large-scale nuclear use unless the Ukraine war shifts significantly, so non-use is likely but conditional.

priorRecord.note: Forecasters put nuclear use in any given year at a few percent at most, though the risk is not zero.

evidenceRecord.note: US intelligence judges Russia will probably keep abiding by the norm against large-scale nuclear use unless the Ukraine war shifts significantly, so non-use is likely but conditional.

claim.text: The erosion of US security guarantees is pushing allies toward nuclear weapons
claim.note: The Bulletin reports that doubts about US extended deterrence have led European states to debate a Euro-deterrent or nuclear latency, and South Korea and Japan to hold similar debates.

priorRecord.note: Public debate about national bombs has grown in Poland, South Korea and elsewhere, but no ally has started a weapons programme.

evidenceRecord.note: The Bulletin reports that doubts about US extended deterrence have led European states to debate a Euro-deterrent or nuclear latency, and South Korea and Japan to hold similar debates.

claim.text: Russia is giving North Korea military technology in return for arms
claim.note: US intelligence says North Korean troops are gaining warfighting experience and military technology from Russia for taking part in the war.

priorRecord.note: US and South Korean officials report Russian help, notably with satellites and air defence, but the extent of the transfers is not publicly verified.

evidenceRecord.note: US intelligence says North Korean troops are gaining warfighting experience and military technology from Russia for taking part in the war.

claim.text: More nuclear-armed states would make the world more dangerous
claim.note: Most scholars argue proliferation raises the odds of accident, theft and use, though a minority argue it spreads stability, and there is no clean test.

priorRecord.note: Most scholars argue proliferation raises the odds of accident, theft and use, though a minority argue it spreads stability, and there is no clean test.

evidenceRecord.note: FRI participants said Iran getting nuclear weapons would raise their risk of nuclear catastrophe by about 50% (experts) or 20% (superforecasters), a non-state actor would double it, and any other new state would raise it 20-30%.

claim.text: China is seeking to become the regional hegemon of Asia
claim.note: US intelligence says China aims to dominate its region and challenge Washington's leadership.

priorRecord.note: China's build-up and pressure on its neighbours fit a bid for regional primacy, but its ultimate aims are a matter of intent that public records only partly show.

evidenceRecord.note: US intelligence says China aims to dominate its region and challenge Washington's leadership.

claim.text: Violence has declined over the long run of human history
claim.note: Homicide and per-capita war deaths fell over centuries in most datasets, though the statistical trend in war deaths is contested.

priorRecord.note: Homicide and per-capita war deaths fell over centuries in most datasets, though the statistical trend in war deaths is contested.

evidenceRecord.note: Cunen et al. find interstate wars got smaller after about 1950 in the Correlates of War data, supporting a decline in war sizes only, with considerable uncertainty.

claim.text: Space-based missile defence could start an arms race in space
